pages.title: APIs - Twenty Documentation
pages.text:
## Schema-per-tenant APIs

There is no static API reference for Twenty. Each workspace has its own schema — when you add a custom object (say `Invoice`), it immediately gets REST and GraphQL endpoints identical to built-in objects like `Company` or `Person`. The API is generated from the schema, so endpoints use your object and field names directly — no opaque IDs.
Your workspace-specific API documentation is available under **Settings → Developers → API** after creating an API key. It includes an interactive playground where you can execute real calls against your data.

## Two APIs

**Core API** — `/rest/` and `/graphql/`
CRUD on records: People, Companies, Opportunities, your custom objects. Query, filter, traverse relations.
**Metadata API** — `/rest/metadata/` and `/metadata/`
Schema management: create/modify/delete objects, fields, and relations. This is how you programmatically change your data model.
Both are available as REST and GraphQL. GraphQL adds batch upserts and the ability to traverse relations in a single query. Same underlying data either way.

## Base URLs

| Environment | Base URL |
| --- | --- |
| Cloud | `https://api.twenty.com/` |
| Self-Hosted | `https://{your-domain}/` |

## Authentication

```
Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
```

Create an API key in **Settings → Developers → API → + Create key**. Copy it immediately — it’s shown once. Keys can be scoped to a specific role under **Settings → Members → Roles → Assignment tab** to limit what they can access.

For OAuth-based access (external apps acting on behalf of users), see OAuth.

## Batch operations

Both REST and GraphQL support batching up to 60 records per request — create, update, or delete. GraphQL also supports batch upsert (create-or-update in one call) using plural names like `CreateCompanies`.

## Selecting fields (REST)

REST record endpoints accept a `fields` query parameter to return only the fields you need:

```
GET /rest/people?fields=id,name,emails,company
```

* `id` is always returned.
* Composite fields (like `emails` or `name`) are selected as a whole by their field name.
* A many-to-one relation field returns its join column (e.g. `companyId`) with `depth=0`. One-to-many relation fields are only returned with `depth=1`. With `depth=1`, only the relation fields listed in `fields` are expanded.
* Unknown fields, or fields your role cannot read, return a `400` error.

When `fields` is omitted on an object with more than 200 readable fields, each record returns a default set of 200 fields: `id`, the label and image identifier fields, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`, `deletedAt`, `position`, then standard fields before custom fields, ordered by name. Pass `fields` explicitly to read any field beyond that default set.

## Rate limits

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Requests | 100 per minute |
| Batch size | 60 records per call |

pages.title: Build on Twenty - Twenty Documentation
pages.text:
## Why build on Twenty

Most CRMs give developers an API and a few places to plug in. Twenty gives you the platform itself. Declare objects, server-side functions, React components and AI agents in plain TypeScript with the `twenty-sdk`, see each change sync to a local server as you save, and ship with the CLI.

* **Manage your workspace with code.** Objects, fields, views and page layouts live as TypeScript files in your repository, versioned and reviewed like any other change.
* **The same SDK as Twenty’s own apps.** Slack, Linear and Granola are apps built with the `twenty-sdk`, so you build with exactly what Twenty’s team uses.
* **Plug into the core, not a sidebar.** Your objects get the same tables and permissions as People and Companies. Your apps can bring conversations into Twenty’s messages, write to record timelines, and expose functions to workflows and AI agents.
* **No ceiling.** The core is open source and self-hostable. When an extension point is missing, change Twenty itself or contribute it back.
* **Safe to experiment.** Apps run sandboxed and only touch the data their role allows, whether your team or an AI agent wrote the code.

## Explore the developer docs

Besides apps, the developer docs cover the API, self-hosting, contributing to Twenty and the UI library.

Apps

Build objects, logic, interfaces and AI agents as TypeScript apps, from quick start to publishing.

API

Read and write records over REST and GraphQL, get webhooks when records change, and connect apps with OAuth.

Self-Host

Run Twenty on your own infrastructure with Docker Compose, then secure and upgrade it.

Contribute

Set up the monorepo locally and help improve the open-source core.

UI Library

Twenty’s open-source React primitives, components, icons and theme tokens.

GitHub

Browse the source code, report issues and follow releases.

Discord

Ask questions and share what you build with the Twenty community.

⌘I

## Authentication

Send a Bearer token with each request:

```http
Authorization: Bearer 
```

Example cURL:

```bash
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ' /rest/core/companies
```

Tokens can be generated in Settings → Playground and are workspace-scoped.

> \*\*Never put your token in a URL.\*\* Tokens passed as query parameters end up in
> server access logs, browser history, and `Referer` headers, which is why the
> API only accepts tokens from the `Authorization` header.


## Filters

Use the `filter` query parameter to narrow results.

- Format: `field[COMPARATOR]:value`
- Multiple conditions: `field1[eq]:1,field2[gte]:10` (root conjunction is AND)
- Composite fields: `field.subField[COMPARATOR]:value`
- Common comparators: `eq`, `neq`, `in`, `containsAny`, `is`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `startsWith`, `like`, `ilike`
- Wildcards: For `like`/`ilike`, use `%` as a wildcard (e.g. `%value%` for substring match)

Examples:

```text
filter=status[eq]:"open"
filter=createdAt[gte]:"2024-01-01"
filter=owner.name[ilike]:"%smith%"
filter=id[in]:["id-1","id-2"]
filter=deletedAt[is]:NULL
filter=isActive[eq]:true
```

Advanced (optional): `and(...)`, `or(...)`, `not(...)` (`not` wraps one condition)

```text
filter=or(status[eq]:"open",assigneeId[is]:NULL)
```

Notes: Strings and dates are quoted; numbers are not.

## Pagination and ordering

All list endpoints use cursor-based pagination.

- Use \*\*limit\*\* to cap page size (default: 60, max: 200).
- Use \*\*starting\_after\*\* to fetch the next page (forward).
- Use \*\*ending\_before\*\* to fetch the previous page (backward).
- Responses include \*\*pageInfo\*\* with `hasNextPage`, `hasPreviousPage`, `startCursor`, and `endCursor`.

Examples:

```bash
# First page
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ' \
 '/rest/core/companies?limit=60'

# Next page
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ' \
 '/rest/core/companies?limit=60&starting\_after='

# Previous page
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ' \
 '/rest/core/companies?limit=60&ending\_before='
```

You can combine pagination with filters and ordering.

Ordering with `order\_by`:
- Shape: `field1,field2[DIRECTION2]`
- Directions: AscNullsFirst, AscNullsLast, DescNullsFirst, DescNullsLast
- Default per-field direction: AscNullsFirst

Examples:
```text
order\_by=createdAt
order\_by=id[AscNullsFirst],createdAt[DescNullsLast]
```

## Usage with LLMs

The recommended way to give an LLM agent (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, …)
access to your workspace is the \*\*Twenty MCP server\*\*, not this OpenAPI schema.
The MCP server exposes typed tools the agent can call directly with proper
header-based auth (OAuth or API key), no tokens in URLs.

Configure it from \*\*Settings → AI → MCP\*\* in your workspace. The endpoint is:

```text
https://api.twenty.com/mcp
```

If you specifically need the raw OpenAPI document (for code generation, type
generation, etc.), download it locally with a header-authenticated request and
hand the file to your tool — never paste a tokenized URL into a chat:

```bash
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer ' \
 https://api.twenty.com/rest/open-api/core > twenty-core.json
```

pages.title: CLI - Twenty Documentation
pages.text:
## Running the CLI

The `twenty` CLI connects to Twenty workspaces from your terminal. Use it to inspect metadata, read records, send API requests, and create, sync and debug apps. The CLI itself requires **Node.js 24.5+**. App development also needs a Node version supported by the installed SDK, see Quick Start.
Run any command through `npx`, without a global installation:

```
npx twenty@latest --version
```

Or install it once globally and call `twenty` directly:

```
npm install -g twenty
twenty --version
```

The examples below use `twenty`. Replace `twenty` with `npx twenty@latest` if you did not install it globally. Run `twenty commands` for the full command list and `twenty <command> --help` for the options of one command.


| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `auth` | Sign in, check and remove credentials |
| `remote` | List, select, rename and remove saved workspace connections |
| `metadata` | Inspect objects and fields |
| `data` | List, read, and export records |
| `api` | Send raw REST or GraphQL requests |
| `open` | Open the workspace in your browser |
| `app` | Create, build, sync, debug and uninstall apps |
| `local` | Start, inspect, stop, upgrade and reset a local development environment |
| `doctor` | Diagnose the CLI, app SDK and workspace connection |

Every command that talks to a workspace accepts `--remote <name>` to target a saved connection other than the default one, and `--json` for structured output.

## Connecting to a workspace

Sign in with your browser. `--use` makes this connection the default one:

```
twenty auth login --url https://acme.twenty.com --use
twenty auth status
```

Use your workspace’s address, or the server’s address for a local setup: `http://localhost:2020` for the local development environment, `http://localhost:3000` for a source checkout. You can copy the exact command from **Settings > Developers > CLI**. Browser sign-in needs Twenty 2.42 or later.
Keep several connections by naming them:

```
twenty auth login --url http://localhost:2020 --name local
twenty remote list
twenty remote use local
```

In CI or scripts, pipe an API key instead of signing in with the browser:

```
printf '%s' "$TWENTY_API_KEY" | twenty auth login --with-token --url https://acme.twenty.com --name ci
```

You can also set `TWENTY_API_URL` and `TWENTY_API_KEY` for a single run without saving anything. Saved connections live in `~/.twenty/config.json`.
Commands select a workspace in this order:

1. An explicit `--remote <name>`, which overrides the target environment variables.
2. `TWENTY_REMOTE`, or the pair `TWENTY_API_URL` and `TWENTY_API_KEY`. Do not combine these two methods.
3. The saved default remote.

`auth login --name <name>` saves a connection but keeps an existing default. Add `--use`, or run `twenty remote use <name>`, to change the default.

### Behind an authenticating proxy

If an identity-aware proxy such as Cloudflare Access, Google IAP, Pomerium or oauth2-proxy sits in front of the server, commands fail with `PROXY_AUTH_REQUIRED`. Give the CLI the proxy’s credentials as headers. Use a command that prints fresh ones, or fixed values for a service token:

```
twenty auth login --url https://twenty.example.com \
  --proxy-header-command 'echo "cf-access-token: $(cloudflared access token -app=https://twenty.example.com)"'

twenty auth login --url https://twenty.example.com \
  --proxy-header "CF-Access-Client-Id: $CLIENT_ID" \
  --proxy-header "CF-Access-Client-Secret: $CLIENT_SECRET"
```

Both are saved on the connection. The command prints one `Name: value` line per header. The CLI runs it again when the proxy rejects the headers, and `PROXY_HEADERS_FAILED` reports a command that fails. In CI, set `TWENTY_PROXY_HEADERS` (one `Name: value` per line) or `TWENTY_PROXY_HEADER_COMMAND` instead. Proxy headers are only sent to the connection’s API URL and cannot replace `Authorization`. See the CLI reference for every option.

## Exploring your data

```
# Objects and fields
twenty metadata object list
twenty metadata field list companies

# Records
twenty data list companies --limit 5
twenty data list companies --filter 'employees[gte]:5000' --order-by 'employees[DescNullsLast]'
twenty data get people <id>

# Raw API requests
twenty api rest '/rest/companies?limit=5'
twenty api graphql --query '{ companies(first: 2) { edges { node { name } } } }'

# Open the workspace, or a page inside it
twenty open
twenty open settings/developers
```

Object names are exact API names, singular or plural (`company` or `companies`). Raw API writes run without a confirmation step, and your permissions in the workspace still apply.

## Building an app

```
npx twenty@latest app init my-app
cd my-app
yarn install
npx twenty@latest app apply --create
npx twenty@latest app dev
```

* `app init` writes a new project from the template. It does not install dependencies or contact a workspace.
* `app apply --create` builds the app, registers it in the workspace, installs it and syncs its metadata.
* `app dev` watches your source and syncs every successful build.

Existing external local files use native filesystem events. Missing or deleted paths use recovery checks once per second until native watching can resume. Home and temporary directory roots and their ancestors are excluded from automatic external directory observation. If `WATCH_SCOPE_LIMITED` appears for a missing import, fix the import, then edit an app file or restart `app dev`.
Run `twenty app dev --verbose` to see watched and excluded paths after the first build attempt and whenever they change. Add `--format ndjson` for structured `watch-scope` progress events.
Other app commands:


| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `app add` | Scaffold an object, field, logic function or other entity |
| `app build` / `app typecheck` | Build or typecheck the app locally |
| `app plan` | Preview the metadata changes an apply would make |
| `app apply` | Build, upload and sync the app |
| `app generate-client` | Regenerate the typed API client without syncing |
| `app pull` | Restore metadata, translations, dependencies, public assets and supported component and logic function source with inventoried local imports |
| `app translations extract` | Extract translatable strings into `locales/` catalogs |
| `app publish` | Publish the app to npm or to a private Twenty registry |
| `app install` | Install an already registered app package in the workspace |
| `app uninstall` | Remove the app and everything it owns from the workspace |

Definitions missing from your source are deleted from the workspace by default. Pass `--no-prune` to keep them. The workspace Custom application keeps them unless you pass `--prune`. Deleting objects or fields also deletes their data, so it requires confirmation. See Syncing & recovery for details.

## Executing functions

Run a deployed logic function without triggering it through a route, a cron or a database event. Sync your local changes with `app apply` or `app dev` first.

```
twenty app exec --name create-new-post-card
twenty app exec --name create-new-post-card --payload '{"name": "Hello"}'

# Install and uninstall hooks
twenty app exec --post-install
twenty app exec --pre-install
twenty app exec --uninstall-hook
```

Executing functions requires a browser sign-in. API keys cannot execute them.

## Watching function logs

Stream the output of your app’s logic functions as executions finish:

```
twenty app logs
twenty app logs --name create-new-post-card
```

It only shows new executions, not past ones.

## Uninstalling an app

```
twenty app uninstall
twenty app uninstall --yes
```

This runs the app’s uninstall hook and deletes everything it owns, including its objects, fields and their data. The app stays registered, so `twenty app apply` can install it again.

## Diagnosing problems

```
twenty doctor
twenty doctor --offline
```

`doctor` checks your Node version, which `twenty` binary is on your `PATH`, your saved connections and the app SDK, then reports what to fix.

## Scripts and tests

Build output belongs to the CLI. Do not read `.twenty/output/manifest.json` or import internal build code; read `data.manifest` from `twenty app build --json`.

## Full reference

The command reference covers every flag, permission, output format and exit code.


## Export workspace records

```
twenty data export companies --output companies.csv
twenty data export companies --fields name,domainName,employees --filter 'employees[gte]:5000' --output large-companies.csv
```

`data export` requires the workspace’s **Export CSV** permission. It follows the server’s export progress, then streams the CSV to `--output`. Record and field permissions are enforced by the server. An app project is not required; select a saved connection with `--remote` or use the usual environment credentials.
The output file appears only after a successful download. Existing files are kept unless you pass `--force`. Downloads are limited to 1 GiB an
